item.title: “Sunrise on the Reaping” Sanitizes and Strips its Source Material of its Radicalness
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

It’s impossible to view The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, the sixth movie in the series, in isolation. The newest movie from director Francis Lawrence (who has directed all of the films after the first) exists fully in the context of the movies that came before it and Suzanne Collins’s books that inspired it all. For those who have been following the series since its inception, Sunrise on the Reaping is low-hanging franchise fruit. Unfortunately, that fruit is overripe with references, the branches of the tree drooping with over a decade of fan-fueled mania.

This latest entry follows Haymitch Abertnathy, played by Joseph Zada, as he competes in the 50th Hunger Games (the second “Quarter Quell”). Fans had been calling for Haymitch’s games since Suzanne Collins announced she was open to writing prequels, with hints of the Second Quarter Quell dropping in Catching Fire. Despite Woody Harrelson’s portrayal of the character being a grumpy alcoholic who does more bullying than mentoring, fans have always felt connected to the character. Haymitch’s movie and book were announced on the same day in 2024, meaning that the film was in development before the book was even published.

Unfortunately, the rush to adapt the book likely dampened the emotional impact of the movie. On paper, Haymitch’s story is devastating. He is thrust into the Hunger Games because he rushes to protect his girlfriend, Lenore Dove (Whitney Peak), as she rushes to the fallen body of the original District 12 tribute, Woodbine Chance, who is gunned down by Peacemakers after he tries to flee the reaping. In need of another tribute, Drusilla Sickle (Glenn Close in prosthetics and some truly incredible wigs) forces sixteen-year-old Haymitch into the games instead. Now, because Haymitch is in the original trilogy, it’s not a spoiler to say that Haymitch wins his games, which also means that he inevitably witnesses the death of (at least) the forty seven other tributes.

Immediately, it becomes clear that everyone involved in running the Hunger Games (and everyone involved in making this movie) is heavily manipulating what’s being shown to the public, altering footage, delaying streams, and rewriting history as it’s happening. Essentially, the whole movie is about propaganda. We know this because it is spelled out for the audience repeatedly, from the mouths of several characters, in almost every scene in the movie, including Jesse Plemmons’ Plutarch Heavensbee, who later becomes instrumental to the overthrowing of the government.

Almost nothing about Sunrise on the Reaping is subtle. The dialogue is heavy-handed, and more than once a character is given full focus as they say their full names, borderline winking at the camera to indicate that they’re someone important in the franchise. This fan service does a major disservice to the themes that have always elevated this series above the stereotypes of its YA genre. At its core, The Hunger Games book series is about radical political action and revolution to overthrow a violent, oppressive government led by a man who has no qualms with killing children in the name of his own power. The central themes of the books are applicable to almost any era of history and any government that relies on propaganda and cruelty to control the masses.

Expecting that kind of radical political theory in a franchise blockbuster produced and created by a major American studio could only ever lead to disappointment. This is a story about the reprehensible ways the government butchered these kids for entertainment, using their bloodshed to remind them of the consequences of revolution. But inherently through making the books into a movie franchise, there is some aspect of audiences using these child actors for entertainment. During the releases of the original trilogy, Jennifer Lawrence and Josh Hutcherson became as huge as Katniss and Peeta themselves—they were carted around the country for our entertainment, giving countless interviews and flirting with each other to ramp up the entertainment levels for the masses. Some of the cast members were given portable cameras to record their journeys leading up to the premiere of The Hunger Games and a significant portion of the footage is them at events with massive crowds of fans cheering for them. This hysteria around the franchise has scaled with the budgets of the films and page counts of the books. And this fanaticism is ultimately what makes the studio its money, so of course that was always going to be the priority here.

For years, people have criticized the movie franchise for being boring outside of the arena, with constant refrains of how it’s always most interesting when the kids are killing each other (often followed by a cheeky comment serving as a feeble attempt to hide the fact that they’re joking about being entertained by children slaughtering each other). This criticism is lazy and demonstrates a failure to engage with the source text. With each entry in the franchise, it becomes more and more clear that although there are of course moments of children choosing to murder each other in hopes of winning the games, the real violence in the arena is often manufactured by President Snow and his legion of Gamemakers. In efforts to keep the games entertaining, the arenas themselves are full of hazards and tools to carry out the government’s slaughter.…

item.title: Where Is Jane Austen in Georgia Oakley’s SENSE AND SENSIBILITY Adaptation?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Books & Culture

Where Is Jane Austen in Georgia Oakley’s SENSE AND SENSIBILITY Adaptation?

For everything that the film does right stylistically and visually, it also gets Austen really wrong

This article is free to read. So is every article Electric Literature publishes. No limits, no paywalls—now or ever. Support from readers like you makes that possible.

We need to raise $60,000 to start off 2027 strong. Donate now to our end of year fundraiser to help ensure the future of free, accessible literature for all.

—————

While a part of me is always surprised when another Austen adaptation comes out, a different part of me—the part that prevails—wants to open the windows and shout Byron from the rooftops: “On with the dance! Let joy be unconfined.”

I suppose I was surprised that there would ever be another big-screen adaptation of Sense and Sensibility for a few reasons. I’ll begin with the reason that is potentially unfair, which is simply that Ang Lee’s 1995 adaptation was done so well I didn’t believe any other would stand up to it. (The 2008 BBC adaptation was solid but forgettable.)

Good adaptations can do that. Beyond being sufficiently powerful to be the “final word” on a work, they can start blending in dangerous and potent ways with the source material. Kate Winslet’s Marianne was Marianne Dashwood, just as Eleanor would always wear the face of Emma Thompson. The 1995 adaptation holds another point of significance for me: I admired the fact that Taiwanese filmmaker Ang Lee was brought on to direct an English period drama set in the late 18th century. Given my compulsion to write about characters and periods that don’t belong to my own time and cultural background, this felt especially important. Certainly, it speaks to the universality of Austen’s appeal, but knowing Lee had directed the film made me, to be frank, rather smug. At the time of my watching the movie, when I was very young and merely pretended to know a lot about Austen, some unspoken barrier seemed to have been lifted. The 1995 Sense and Sensibility movie was a truly great film on its own, a masterly adaptation of one of Austen’s most beloved works, and it was also directed by Ang Lee.

But none of this answers my original question of why Austen continues to be adapted again and again—and again. The cynical part of me finds it concerning, if not eyebrow-raising, that in our modern age, part of the continued appeal may be that we are still buying into the fantasy of uncomplicated happy endings, of simple love stories that treat love as an uncomplex and straightforward entity when it is anything but. Love is complicated (how can it not be?) because it is an amalgam of human quirks, of individual traumas and socio-economic backgrounds, of professions and different belief systems—the list can go on and on of all the factors that make a personality what it is. Still, many consider Austen to be light fare, ascribing her to the realm of the lovey-dovey and sentimental. It’s all about romance and love, isn’t it? So it has to be feel-good and happy. It’s all about stupid misunderstandings, but in the end, the guy gets the girl, right? Wrong.

I thought of this when I watched Georgia Oakley’s Sense and Sensibility, starring Daisy Edgar -Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles as Eleanor and Marianne Dashwood. Oakley reminds us Austen deserves to be taken seriously. Very seriously. No light fare to be had here. From the get-go, everything feels an uphill battle for our lovely protagonists. The very first scene throws the viewer into a state of tension. Marianne lies in grass, watching a caterpillar crawl across her finger. It looks languid and pretty, the kind of scene one expects to lead an Austen film (rather like Keira Knightley’s Elizabeth Bennet taking a leisurely walk at the beginning of Pride and Prejudice while reading the final pages of a book). Appearances can be deceiving, however. Marianne is actually waiting for the mail coach that brings her father’s will. The scene of Marianne starting up from the grass when the coach appears and running towards it is interspersed with a beautiful visual of fallow deer running. Symbolically, this works well. The film often asks the question of who is really doing the hunting. Is it the men, who make offers of marriage? Or the women, endowed or, as is the unfortunate case with Eleanor and Marianne, not endowed with any significant fortune or estate? The Dashwood sisters are equipped with only their beauty and personal charms to find husbands. A much later scene of a heartbroken Marianne wandering the woods brings this point home. Her spirit subdued, she comes across a pack of hounds that run past, ignoring her. It’s an eerie and rather dark moment in the film that shows the extent to which Marianne’s passion and life force have literally been drained by the pursuit of love. Despite her vivacity and quick intelligence, she has never been the hunter or predator but always the quarry, the coveted hind.

For everything that the film does right stylistically and visually, it also gets Austen really wrong. This isn’t only because the men of the film were so forgettable that I’m convinced cardboard cutouts would do just as well (as for Edgar-Jones and Creed-Miles, they were a delight to watch). But by taking the “Austen” out of the business of love and marriage, the adaptation seems to miss the point. In Oakley’s film, we see all the difficulties and challenges of love and marriage without being able to laugh at any of it. This makes things not only dreary but also uninteresting. Without humor, without lightness and wit, we have a very basic story of two sisters whose financially straitened circumstances render it a matter of both urgency and necessity to seek husbands. One sister (Eleanor) is more rational, more levelheaded, while the younger (Marianne) is outwardly more passionate. Time is of the essence. Youth and beauty won’t last forever. The clock is always ticking.…

item.title: 17 films to see before New Year's, from Oscar-bait to blockbusters
item.description:

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

17 films to see before New Year's, from Oscar-bait to blockbusters

The movies see before New Year's, from Oscar-bait to blockbusters

Hollywood's heading into the holidays on a high note. Odysseus and Spider-Man led cinemas to the biggest summer ever at the box office. Since then, studio hits have been jockeying with indie surprises like You Can See Everything. In theaters this Thanksgiving are Focker-in-Law, Club Kid, the Rocky origin story, another unforgettable Andrew Scott performance, a Hunger Games sequel and more.

But Tinseltown may have saved the best — or at least the buzziest — for last. Here's what else is coming between now and year's end.

Behemoth!

In theaters Dec. 4

Pedro Pascal spent months practicing cello many hours a day so he'd look convincing playing a cello in the fictional drama Behemoth!, about a musician whose personal life gets in the way of his art.

The Gallerist

In theaters Dec. 4

Artistic temperaments are in comic opposition in The Gallerist, in which struggling art gallery owner Natalie Portman spars with art influencer Zach Galifianakis, who clearly has it in for her. When he accidentally trips and skewers himself on a very sharp sculpture —and dies just before the gallery's public opening — she decides she has little choice but to try to pass him off as conceptual art.

Jane Elliott Against the World

In Los Angeles and New York starting on Dec. 4

In 1968, Jane Elliott came up with a classroom exercise to help elementary school kids understand the unfairness of racism: "blue-eyed people are better than brown-eyed people," she told the kids. For that lesson, she got both fame and hate mail. In the documentary Jane Elliott Against the World, she's still going strong, sharing the lessons she learned back then. The film will also be shown on PBS Independent Lens on March 29, 2027.

Everybody Digs Bill Evans

In New York starting Dec. 4, expands in January

The title of the jazzy bio-pic Everybody Digs Bill Evans certainly qualifies as truth-in-advertising: Evans (Anders Danielsen Lie) had a difficult life, but he made glorious music. Laurie Metcalf and Bill Pullman play his folks.

George Michael: The Faith Tour

In theaters and IMAX Dec. 11

Never-released footage of the singer-songwriter George Michael led to this concert film, captured over two nights in Paris in 1988 on his first headlining solo tour.

Tender Loving Care

In Los Angeles and New York on Dec. 11, then expanding in December and into January

During the workday, the social workers in Tender Loving Care face clients who claim they don't need any help; when they're off the clock, it's aging family members. 83-year-old filmmaker Mike Leigh says Tender Loving Care will be his final film, and a lovely, elegiac one it is.

Ink

In theaters Dec. 11 and on Netflix Jan. 8

This journalism saga charts the 1960s rise of news mogul Rupert Murdoch, played here by a brash Guy Pearce, who altered Britain's staid news landscape when he bought a London tabloid. Jack O'Connell plays The Sun editor Larry Lamb, Claire Foy a reporter, and director Danny Boyle tells the story with tabloid-esque flair.

The Debut

In limited theaters Dec. 11

In Jesse Eisenberg's warmly funny comedy, Julianne Moore and Paul Giamatti play, respectively, a timid housewife who tries out for a musical ("I haven't sung in front of anyone since church choir") and the tyrannical director who's the self-styled "biggest name in New Jersey community theater." Watching Moore pretend to be a bad actor is fascinating.

Rose

In theaters Dec. 11

Sandra Hüller disguises herself as a man to fight in a 17th century war, then continues to live as a man so she can inherit a neglected country estate, even though that means she must marry and somehow hide her true identity from her wife.

Avengers: Doomsday

In theaters Dec. 18

In an unprecedented battle-of-the-blockbusters that industry-watchers are calling "Dunes-Day," Marvel's superhero showdown opens on the same day as the sci-fi spectacle Dune: Part Three. With Dune having locked down every single IMAX theater for the first three weeks, Marvel has rebranded other premium-format screens so that the Avengers can play in what the company is calling "Infinity Vision."

Dune: Part Three

In theaters and IMAX Dec. 18

The finale to Denis Villeneuve's intergalactic trilogy corresponds roughly with Frank Herbert's second novel, Dune Messiah, in which Maud'Dib (Timothée Chalamet) realizes that after years of war, he's become the oppressor that Chani (Zendaya) is fighting.

Clarissa

In New York and Los Angeles Dec. 18 for one week, opens again in theaters in January

Taking stabs at the patriarchy in a serious way is Sophie Okonedo in this ruminative drama, which transplants Virginia Woolf's feminist novel Mrs. Dalloway to contemporary Nigeria. Ayo Edebiri and David Oyelowo offer support.

Artificial

In limited theaters Dec. 25, everywhere Jan. 8

Filmmaker Luca Guadagnino has Andrew Garfield play Open AI creator Sam Altman as a kind of seductive vampire of a tech-bro in a film that will not reassure anybody about the future of AI. It explores what happened when tech guys who'd said they wanted to keep the world safe from artificial intelligence decided they'd just as soon make money off it.

Werwulf

In theaters Dec. 25

Director Robert Eggers, who recently gave us a gothic-horror vampire in Nosferatu, brings another supernatural critter to life in this black-and-white art film. Aaron Taylor-Johnson sprouts fangs, Willem Dafoe's the huntsman.

Jumanji: Open World

In theaters Dec. 25

In this family-oriented sequel, instead of players getting pulled into the Jumanji game, critters from the game escape into the real world. So do some mixed-up avatars. This time, Spencer's mother Janice takes the form of Dwayne Johnson's Dr. Smolder Bravestone, and Kevin Hart embodies 7-year-old Tyson ("except I'm a Black grownup").

Coward

In theaters Dec. 25…

item.title: Fear is the Mind Killer: Comics for DUNE Fans
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Fear is the Mind Killer: Comics for DUNE Fans

The books are long, and the new movies directed by Denis Villeneuve are so good. I have found success reading the Dune series through comics though.

Frank Herbert’s son, Brian Herbert, along with Kevin J. Anderson, have adapted the iconic series into graphic novel format. These books have given me a satisfying taste of the story paired with beautiful art of the desolate yet mesmerizing world of Dune.

The series includes three volumes, Dune: The Graphic Novel Book 1, Book 2: Muad’Dib, and Book 3: The Prophet. The gorgeous illustrations by Raúl Allén and Patricia Martín immerse you right into the landscape of the bleak and breathtaking desert planet. The character art is compelling and helps show their feelings and motivations, rather than just tell them through narrative.

The new Dune film, Dune: Part Three, releases in theaters December 18th. While the Dune graphic novels offer a great way to catch up on the series before you see the movie, I also have comics for Dune fans who want to fall into similar stories.

Each comic below touches upon various themes that make Dune special. Between their pages, you’ll travel across wasteland planets crawling with curious creatures, immerse in political intrigue amongst warring nobility, and follow space wanderers on desperate quests.

Comics for Dune Fans

Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind by Hayao Miyazaki

Hayao Miyazaki’s manga series is a must-read for Dune fans. Like Paul Atreides, Nausicaä steps into a prophesied savior role in her story, though Nausicaä strives for peace over war. Her world shares many similarities with Dune, with its barren landscapes and powerful Ohmu creatures reminiscent of Dune’s sandworms. As various kingdoms wage war on each other in an effort to control ancient, destructive technology, Nausicaä sets out to try and negotiate peace.

Count by Ibrahim Moustafa

Alexandre Dumas’s The Count of Monte Cristo is a classic tale of corruption, oppression, and revenge, and these themes strongly align with the story of Dune. Ibrahim Moustafa does an incredible job of adapting Dumas’s classic into a sci-fi graphic novel. After getting framed for treason and locked away in a hover-prison, Redxan Samud makes his great escape, puts his new fortune to use, and seeks revenge on those who ruined his life.

Monstress, Volume 1: Awakening by Marjorie M. Liu, Illustrated by Sana Takeda

This epic graphic novel by Marjorie M. Liu includes stunning illustrations by Sana Takeda. The story takes place in an alternate matriarchal 1900’s Asia. Like Paul Atreides, teen Maika possesses powerful psychic abilities. As Maika tries to survive in a dark, war-stricken world, she navigates a curious connection to a monster that will put them both in danger.

On a Sunbeam by Tillie Walden

While this sweet graphic novel by Tillie Walden offers a more quietly-paced sci-fi story than Dune, it does include the theme of searching for someone across space. Just as the Bene Gesserit seek the Kwisatz Haderach in Dune, the protagonist in this book, Mia, looks for her long-lost love. Fans of the epic cinematography of the Dune movies and the vivid descriptions of sci-fi landscapes in the Dune books will also appreciate the breathtaking art of this moving graphic novel.

Like Dune, I hope these comics offer you windows into awe-inspiring and compelling sci-fi worlds. For more good reads for Dune fans, check out these 14 Fascinating Books Like DUNE, or these Best Science Fiction Books of the Century (So Far).

item.title: The jewels of Route 66: Neon signs are making a comeback
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

The jewels of Route 66: Neon signs are making a comeback

During its heyday, Route 66 became an iconic road trip, connecting the main streets of cities and small towns from Chicago to Los Angeles. And neon signs were the radiant jewels scattered along the roadside.

The glowing glass lights were a fairly new thing when Route 66 opened in November 1926. Parisian Georges Claude had invented the idea of running electricity through tubing filled with neon gas in 1910. The first neon sign arrived in the U.S. in 1922, at a Packard car dealership, and locals were wonderstruck. Reportedly, gapers caused traffic jams.

Claude sold franchises, including one to what is now Claude Neon Federal Signs, founded 100 years ago, just like Route 66. It's still in operation in Tulsa, and the company's website says it's the largest sign company in Oklahoma.

Neon: beautiful and dangerous

CNF Signs still has "neon benders" — artisans who heat glass tubes in a fire and bend the glass by hand to form shapes and letters, just as Claude did. One of them is Tom Wolski, who said he tells visitors to his studio to stand way back.

"In this room you have extreme electricity. You have fire, you have phosphorus, you have mercury. It is kind of dangerous; you have to pay attention to what you're doing. God knows why I would want to do this, but I love it," Wolski said, laughing.

He was once one of two full-time neon benders at CNF Signs, but fewer and fewer companies have commissioned them, because they're so expensive.

Instead, many are turning to LEDs, which can seem like neon. LEDS are less expensive to make and operate and are less dangerous. But Joe Kesterson, senior designer at CNF Signs, maintains that LEDs are not as beautiful.

Neon glows, like a candle, he explained. LED lights are brighter and sharper.

It may be easy to mistake LED lights for neon lights, he added, but "once you see both of them together, you can see [the LEDs] have almost a harshness to the light."

An interesting fact: Neon lights themselves are not all neon gas.

"Neon gas is red when it illuminates," Kesterson said. "And so anything that you see that's got a warm color is usually going to have neon in it. But cool colors are made using argon gas."

Plus a couple of beads of mercury, which keeps the gas's molecules unstable and energized.

The argon-and-mercury combination interacts with a phosphor powder coating on the inside of some tubes, which makes them glow in a rainbow of colors.

"And it never works like you think it would," Kesterson said. "It's not like we learned in school, where blue and yellow make green. If I put blue gas in a yellow piece of neon, a lot of times it's orange or some weird color that you would not expect."

From migrants to vacationers

Those bright colors "are part of the mystique of Route 66," Kesterson said. "That's what you would have seen traveling as a child with your parents across the country."

Route 66 was the country's first paved highway and served as the primary route for migrating farmworkers during the Dust Bowl. Later, it became a military transport corridor during World War II. All that traffic led to gas stations, restaurants and motels, and those amenities led to vacationers.

"And as you're flying down that highway, you need something that is going to stop that business and bring them to your doorstep," said Kathleen Franz, the associate director for curatorial affairs at the National Museum of American History and a specialist in the history of technology.

"Businesses that had neon seemed up-to-date, modern, new. Here's a business willing to invest in itself."

And that, Franz said, signified to travelers that the motel or restaurant was clean and safe. Suddenly, neon was everywhere. And it was inventive.

The 1950s brought Googie-style signs with Space Age shapes: boomerangs and parabolas, stars and swirls. Companies learned how to animate their signs, to make flashing arrows and looping lassos.

Tulsa was a place that went particularly big. The 1934 "Meadow Gold" sign, a local landmark advertising a dairy, is the size of a school bus, with letters up to 7 feet high. It was originally built by Claude Neon Federal Signs, and they restored it about 70 years later.

A decline and rebirth

Over time, five new interstate highways replaced portions of Route 66, and it stopped being recognized entirely as a federal highway in 1985. Small town traffic dwindled, and businesses closed. Neon signs are expensive to run, and many were turned off, sold, trashed or, like the Meadow Gold sign, stored.

But almost immediately, a movement started to preserve and commemorate the road, and in 1999, a law authorized the National Park Service Route 66 Corridor Preservation Program. Along the old route, communities hoping to draw back those tourists started restoring roadside attractions, including neon signs.

In 2004, the Meadow Gold sign was saved when the building it was on was slated for demolition. CNF Signs rebuilt the scaffolding and restored the porcelain letters that house the neon; it was relit and placed in what is now the Meadow Gold section of town in 2009.

In 2019, looking toward the Route 66 centennial, the Tulsa Route 66 Commission started a grant program for businesses that wanted to make new signs out of neon or LED tubing, or restore old ones. Now, there are more than 100 neon signs in Tulsa, including re-created vintage ones in Neon Sign Park, part of Cyrus Avery Plaza.

Those replicas include signs otherwise lost to history, like the Will Rogers Motor Court, with a cowboy on a rearing horse (The name "Will Rogers" is circled by a gold lasso), and the Tulsa Auto Court, which features a red car with a driver's silhouette in the window and what seem to be moving tires.

The park is on a very quiet section of Route 66, next to a river and train tracks and below the interstate. Above it, traffic whizzes by on I-244.

You can't see the signs from the modern highway, but they're there, glowing.…

item.title: 'All of a Sudden' is over 3 hours long. Our critic can't wait to see it a third time
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Review

Review

Movie Reviews

'All of a Sudden' is over 3 hours long. Our critic can't wait to see it a third time

For much of the new movie All of a Sudden, we are in a for-profit elder-care facility in suburban Paris, which is run by a smart, forward-thinking director named Marie-Lou, played by Virginie Efira.

Marie-Lou is training her staff in the techniques of Humanitude, a real-life methodology that stresses compassionate, hands-on caregiving, especially for patients with dementia. But training costs time and resources, and some of Marie-Lou's overworked staff reject the Humanitude approach.

This might not sound like a gripping premise, but the Japanese writer-director Ryûsuke Hamaguchi has spun it into something extraordinary. I shouldn't be too surprised at this point. His earlier dramas, like Happy Hour, Wheel of Fortune and Fantasy and Drive My Car, remind us that a scene of two people talking in a mundane setting can be as deeply transporting as anything in cinema.

Hamaguchi writes gorgeously enveloping dialogue that flows naturally even as it bristles with ideas. When I recently profiled him for The New Yorker, he told me that All of a Sudden was influenced by some of our greatest and talkiest filmmakers. It combines the institutional texture of a Frederick Wiseman documentary with the conversational flow of an Éric Rohmer romance.

Early on in the film, Marie-Lou meets a Japanese woman named Mari, played by Tao Okamoto. The similarity of their names suggests that this is a fateful encounter; so does the fact that each one can speak the other's primary language fluently. (To prepare for their roles, Efira learned Japanese and Okamoto studied French — just one impressive aspect of their beautifully synched performances.)

Mari is in Paris directing an experimental play that addresses mental-health care issues — a subject that overlaps with Marie-Lou's work. The two women spend a long night walking around Paris and talking about their dreams, their backgrounds and their desire to make the world a better place.

But as Marie-Lou knows firsthand from her work with Humanitude, it's hard to effect meaningful change in an environment that has to deal with administrative challenges, staffing shortages and low morale. At one point, while hanging out one-on-one with Marie-Lou at the nursing home, Mari uses a whiteboard to diagram her insights into the impact of capitalism on workers — a sequence that might sound didactic on paper but is utterly riveting to watch and listen to. It's a reminder that filmmakers too rarely trust their characters, or their audiences, to grapple with complex ideas.

The title All of a Sudden could describe how quickly Marie-Lou and Mari become soulmates, not in a romantic sense, but in an intellectual and philosophical one. Yet the title also captures how swiftly life can slip away. Hamaguchi and his co-writer, Léa Le Dimna, adapted the script from a nonfiction book, consisting of letters exchanged by two women, one of whom died from cancer shortly before the book was published.

In the film, Mari reveals early on that she is terminally ill, which means that we're witnessing both the beginning and the end of a beautiful friendship. Is it a cruelty or a miracle that they met under these circumstances? Maybe a bit of both.

I've seen a lot of end-of-life movies in my life as a critic, but never one quite like All of a Sudden. Hamaguchi is both realistic and empathetic; he's neither sentimental nor cynical. Both his protagonists have to learn to accept their limitations.

Only when Marie-Lou has grace on herself and her staff does she realize how much good they can do, even within their very real constraints. And only when Mari comes to terms with the fact that she's dying can she really live each moment to the fullest. As the story draws to a close, Hamaguchi seems to push his characters in bold and exploratory new directions. The less time we have with them, the more vivid they become.

Here's where I should note that All of a Sudden runs about three-and-a-quarter hours — and that it feels shorter than some two-hour movies. The length is deliberate, but it isn't indulgent. It takes time to really get to know someone, Hamaguchi seems to be saying, fictional characters included.

Giving of your time can be draining, but it can also be restorative. I've seen All of a Sudden twice, and I'm looking forward to a third viewing. The hours I've spent getting to know Marie-Lou and Mari are the most rewarding I've had in a movie theater this year.

4 Immersive South Asian Fantasy Novels

Below, she recommends three more fantasy novels inspired by South Asia.

South Asian fantasy is more than the narrative equivalent of mango lassi and butter chicken: While you’ll never see me turn down these now-classic dishes, the truth is that there’s so much more to this diverse region to explore, especially when it comes to books. It’s been so amazing for me, as an American author of Pakistani descent, to see the different ways that authors of South Asian origin have been channeling their myriad inspirations to create new worlds, develop compelling characters, and tell stories that stay with you long after you’ve turned the last page.

My book, The Peacock Throne, is a riff on the Anastasia story about an orphan who thinks that she’s really the long-lost princess of her colonized country and will do anything to find out if she’s right. And in my case, as well as those of the amazing books in this list, South Asia is more than the cherry on top of the sundae (or, to keep it on theme, the basil seeds on top of the falooda): It’s the whole dessert.

The Candle and the Flame by Nafiza Azad

This lyrical, stirring novel stars Fatima, one of the few human survivors of a massacre in the city of Noor who must save the city from a terrible conspiracy. Though it’s located on the Silk Road, Noor most closely resembles a diverse South Asian city, and it’s so beautifully realized that it makes you feel nostalgic even as you’re still getting to know it.

The Silver Kingdom by Radiya Hafiza

This new dual-POV South Asian romantasy is a book after my heart. Set in a world inspired by the Indian subcontinent after it was divided into two and then three independent countries, it takes the tropes you know and love—Chosen One prophecies, warring kingdoms, forbidden lovers—and applies them to a new postcolonial context that feels fresh and modern.

Monsters Born and Made by Tanvi Berwah

The righteous anger of this book’s main character, Koral, as she forces herself into the upper class’s chariot race (featuring the monstrous maristags), draws you through a world that might seem like no South Asian fantasy you’ve read before. But its critique of caste and class pushes the bounds of what a South Asian fantasy can look like, and does it with a ton of pulse-pounding action.

A dish with a story, Thanksgiving with culinary historian Michael Twitty

Culinary historian Michael Twitty on tracing familial connections through food

This Thanksgiving, Morning Edition host Leila Fadel left the studio for her kitchen, where she was met by the two-time James Beard Award winner Michael Twitty, who came with a spice blend, fresh sage, fish peppers and onions from his garden.

His book, The Cooking Gene, planted him as one of the nation's foremost chronologists tracing his ancestry through African American culinary history.

Kush, the forerunner to Southern cornbread dressing

Kush is one of Twitty's most beloved Thanksgiving offerings and one he's been making since he was a teen. The name and the ingredients show the way food became a tool for the enslaved in the Americas to preserve their cultures.

"The name comes from Hausa, the language of West Africa. They are a predominantly Muslim people, but Muslim in the way that West Africans do Islam – which is Islam with a lot of the influence from the traditional culture and spirituality," he said on the origins of the side dish. "And so the name Kush, it's like, couscous," he added.

The dish is one that connects Twitty to his ancestry.

"There was a time when I couldn't tell you what particular African ethnic groups I came from, but now that I know that I'm part Wolof, Hausa, Fula, and Serer and so many others," he said. "Now, I know this dish has a connection to who I am and my roots and where I came from."

In the making of this dish, Twitty also shared his work documenting the ways African American Jewish people create hybrid dishes in the kitchen.

"It's Matzah ball gumbo, and it's black-eyed peas and quiche," he said of his Black and Jewish identity. "It's a lot of dishes that were from North Africa or from Ethiopia, it's kosher jollof rice and Shito. Shito usually has shellfish in it – we don't put that."

What Thanksgiving and this dish mean to Twitty

The author of four books tracing the deep roots of the foods he loves says for him it's less about the lore of Thanksgiving, and more about the people the day brings together.

"I have to say that along with a lot of other African Americans, not everybody, but a plurality of us, Thanksgiving, as it's been expressed, means very little," he said of the holiday. "Which means we're not attaching ourselves to the myth of Thanksgiving, we don't really care for that. But we do love tradition, we love cooking, we love food, we love gathering."

And in that spirit, Kush in particular, remains one way for him to taste history.

"It means I haven't forgotten who I come from. And it means I haven't forgotten that I have a legacy to leave," he said.

You can find the recipe for Twitty's Kush in his book, Recipes from the American South.
